lead: A medical device may be sold only after its risk class decides how much evidence it needs and which licence it must hold. The rule chain asks: does it enter the body, how long does it stay, and how much energy or fluid does it deliver? India uses four classes, A to D, under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, run by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO). The US uses three classes, with 510(k) substantial-equivalence review and premarket approval. Europe uses the CE mark. Only a few universities teach this.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.5, because the electrical safety standard appears inside the regulatory file.

blocks.text: Classification predicts harm, not quality. A tongue depressor touches skin and does nothing else. A pacemaker sits in the heart for years and can deliver current. The same failure is not equally dangerous, so the evidence cannot be equal.

Indian rules use a rule chain. Ask three questions in order. Does the device enter the body? How long does it stay? Does it deliver energy or medicine? Duration has three bands: transient under 60 minutes, short-term from 60 minutes to 30 days, long-term over 30 days. The answers send the device to class A, B, C or D. Class A is low risk. Class D is high risk. Higher class means more documents: risk analysis, bench data, clinical evaluation, and often clinical investigation. The class also decides who licenses the device. A sterile syringe and an implantable pacemaker can both be single-use, but they do not carry the same risk.

sections.h3: India, the US, Europe and standards

blocks.text: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) administers the Medical Devices Rules, 2017. A device needs a licence to be manufactured, imported, sold or distributed. For manufacture, Class A and B licences come from the State Licensing Authority and Class C and D licences from the Central Licensing Authority. Import licences for all four classes come from the Central Licensing Authority (CDSCO). Sale and distribution licences are issued by the State Licensing Authority.

The quality system must follow ISO 13485. Risk management must follow ISO 14971. Electrical safety is proved against IEC 60601-1, the standard from Chapter 6.5. Clinical evaluation supports the claimed benefit. After sale, the manufacturer runs post-market surveillance and reports adverse events to CDSCO.

The US Food and Drug Administration uses three classes. Class I needs general controls. Class II needs special controls and usually a 510(k) premarket notification, which shows substantial equivalence to a predicate device already legally marketed in the United States. Class III needs premarket approval (PMA) with clinical data. Europe uses the CE mark under the EU Medical Device Regulation. Higher classes need a notified body to audit the quality system and technical file. The CE mark is valid for Europe; it does not replace an Indian licence. Labelling and instructions for use state intended use, warnings and sterilisation steps.

figure.caption: A device touching skin goes to class A or B; a device entering the body goes to class B for transient use, and to class C or D for longer use or implants; class D carries the heaviest evidence.

spec.aria: Decision tree that sends a non-invasive device to class A or B; an invasive device used transiently goes to class B, and longer use or an implant goes to class C or D.

examples.question: Assign an Indian risk class to each device and give its evidence rank, where class A = 1, B = 2, C = 3, D = 4. (i) reusable stainless-steel tongue depressor, (ii) sterile single-use hypodermic syringe, (iii) implantable cardiac pacemaker. Which needs the most evidence?
steps: Tongue depressor: non-invasive, touches skin, delivers no energy or fluid. Class A. Evidence rank 1.
Syringe: invasive, enters the body, transient use for an injection. Class B. Evidence rank 2.
Pacemaker: implantable, long-term contact, delivers electrical energy. Class D. Evidence rank 4.
Highest rank is 4: the pacemaker needs the most evidence, including clinical investigation and long-term follow-up.
examples.answer: Tongue depressor class A (rank 1), syringe class B (rank 2), pacemaker class D (rank 4); the pacemaker needs the most evidence.

traps: Price or brand does not set the class. Class follows invasiveness, contact duration and energy delivered.
A CE mark does not replace an Indian licence. The device still needs CDSCO licensing under the 2017 rules.
Sterility alone does not make a syringe class C. A single-use syringe is invasive for transient use, so class B.
IEC 60601-1 proves electrical safety only. It is not the full technical file or clinical evidence.

quiz.q: What does CDSCO stand for, and which rules govern Indian medical devices?
quiz.a: Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation; Medical Devices Rules, 2017.

quiz.q: Why does a pacemaker need more evidence than a tongue depressor?
quiz.a: Pacemaker: invasive, long-term, delivers energy, class D. Tongue depressor: non-invasive, no energy, class A. Higher class needs more clinical and post-market evidence.

quiz.q: A sterile single-use scalpel enters the body for less than 60 minutes and delivers no energy. Which Indian class?
A thermometer has a CE mark. Can it be sold in India without an Indian licence?
quiz.a: No. The CE mark is European. India requires a CDSCO licence, issued by the State or Central Licensing Authority by class.

quiz.q: Name the quality-system standard and the risk-management standard.
quiz.a: ISO 13485 for quality; ISO 14971 for risk.
Substantial equivalence to a legally marketed device; not full premarket approval.

beyond: Not for the exam. Regulators now discuss unique device identification, electronic instructions for use, and software as a medical device. AI/ML diagnostic software needs a planned change-control route in some markets. Global harmonisation is led by the International Medical Device Regulators Forum. Search for IMDRF, EU MDR, FDA digital health and the CDSCO medical device portal.
